screens.title: Setting Up Your First XR Project in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn how to configure a Unity project for both AR and VR, install the essential packages, set up XR Plugin Management, and prepare build and player settings so your app can run on Android devices and PC or Quest headsets. We'll also walk through creating a minimal AR scene that places objects on detected planes and a simple VR rig using the XR Interaction Toolkit. This setup work is crucial: without the right packages and provider selections, Unity cannot communicate with ARCore, ARKit, OpenXR, or device-specific runtimes. For example, AR Foundation provides the common A P I but needs platform providers like ARCore or ARKit to actually detect planes on a phone. Throughout this lesson you'll see concrete steps to avoid common mistakes such as forgetting to switch platforms, not enabling the correct plugin provider, or misconfiguring scripting and architecture for Android builds. By the end you'll understand the project-level decisions that let your scenes initialize XR at startup and run reliably on target hardware. Think about a simple test: placing a cube on a detected plane. If that works on your device, your pipeline is correctly configured.

Setting Up Your First XR Project in Unity

This chapter shows the exact packages to install, how to enable XR providers for Android and Standalone, and the build and player settings needed for ARCore, ARKit, OpenXR and Meta devices. It ends with two practical scene templates: a tappable AR placement flow and a minimal VR origin.

screens.title: Package Manager and Essential Packages
screens.narratorSegment: The Package Manager is where Unity grows into an XR-capable editor. Think of it as a repository of editor extensions and runtime libraries that add AR and VR features. Start by switching the Package Manager view to the Unity Registry so you see official packages. The key packages to install are XR Plugin Management, which centralizes provider configuration; AR Foundation, which offers a cross-platform AR A P I; OpenXR, which gives a device-agnostic VR interface; and the platform-specific provider packages like ARCore XR Plugin for Android and ARKit XR Plugin for iOS. Install the XR Interaction Toolkit if you'll build VR interactions. A concrete example: installing AR Foundation alone won’t make plane detection work on Android — ARCore XR Plugin is needed so the phone’s AR runtime can be accessed. A common misconception is that a single package covers all platforms; instead, AR Foundation is the bridge and platform providers are the engines. After installation, verify package versions and restart the editor if package dependencies require it. This reduces mysterious runtime errors and ensures the Package Manager shows the provider packages as available in Project Settings when you configure XR Plugin Management.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Package Manager
Install the essential XR packages
Open Window > Package Manager, choose Unity Registry, and install the packages below in order.
Step-by-step
  1. Open Package Manager and switch to Unity Registry.
  2. Install XR Plugin Management first so Project Settings shows the XR tab.
  3. Install AR Foundation and OpenXR Plugin next.
  4. Install platform providers: ARCore XR Plugin for Android, ARKit XR Plugin for iOS, Meta/Oculus plugins as needed.
  5. If building VR interactions, install XR Interaction Toolkit.
Why order matters
  • XR Plugin Management creates the configuration UI where providers appear.
  • AR Foundation exposes APIs that rely on platform providers for runtime access to hardware.
  • Install providers early so dependencies resolve and Editor warnings are minimized.
Key Takeaway

AR Foundation is the cross-platform API; provider packages are required to actually run AR on devices.

Package list (visual)
XR Plugin Management
OpenXR Plugin
AR Foundation
ARCore XR Plugin / ARKit XR Plugin
Meta/Oculus or vendor plugins
Concrete example
If you want plane detection on Android: install AR Foundation and ARCore XR Plugin, then enable ARCore in XR Plugin Management under Android. Without ARCore selected, AR Foundation cannot access the device's AR runtime and plane detection won't work.
Common mistake
Installing only AR Foundation and assuming plane detection will work on a phone. ARCore or ARKit must also be installed and enabled per platform.

screens.title: Configure XR Plugin Management
screens.narratorSegment: XR Plugin Management is the bridge between Unity and device runtimes. Open Edit > Project Settings > XR Plugin Management and you'll see tabs for each target platform, such as Android and Standalone. For an Android AR build, select the Android tab and enable ARCore. For Quest or other Meta devices running Android, enable Oculus or OpenXR depending on your chosen provider. On Standalone, enable OpenXR or Oculus for PC-focused VR. A concrete example: if you want to target Meta Quest using OpenXR, enable OpenXR in the Android tab and also configure any necessary runtime features in the OpenXR settings. A frequent misconception is to only install the plugin but forget to toggle it on per-platform; remember that installation makes providers available, while XR Plugin Management activates them for a specific platform. Also check the option to initialize XR on startup for the platform — without it, you may need to initialize subsystems manually in code. Finally, after changing providers, restart the Editor when prompted to ensure native bindings are loaded. This step often resolves mysterious initialization failures during builds.

keyIdea.text: Installing a provider is not enough; enable it in XR Plugin Management per platform and enable initialization so the runtime can start automatically.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › XR Plugin Management
Enable provider per platform
Providers must be enabled under the platform tab so Unity initializes the correct XR SDK when building or running.
Checklist
  • Select the target platform tab (Android or Standalone).
  • Check the provider you installed, e.g., ARCore for Android or OpenXR for Standalone.
  • Enable "Initialize XR on Startup" for automatic initialization.
  • Restart the Editor if requested to load native bindings.
Misconception
Do not assume installing ARCore registers it automatically for all platforms. You must enable it in the Android tab. Installation makes it available; XR Plugin Management enables it for a platform.
Key Takeaway

Provider must be active for the platform you build; enabling per-platform is the step that lets Unity talk to the device runtime.

Visual: platform tabs
Android tab — providers: ARCore (checked)
Standalone tab — providers: OpenXR (checked)
Toggle: Initialize XR on Startup (checked)
Concrete example
To target Meta Quest via OpenXR: enable OpenXR in the Android tab and ensure any required OpenXR features are set in the OpenXR settings. Confirm the runtime initializes by testing on device after a build.
Troubleshooting hint
If the app shows a blank screen on Quest, confirm the Android tab has the correct provider enabled and that "Initialize XR on Startup" is checked. Also verify Package Name and architecture in Player Settings.

screens.title: Build Settings and Player Settings for Android AR
screens.narratorSegment: Build Settings and Player Settings determine whether an Android APK will install and run AR features. To prepare for ARCore, open File > Build Settings and switch the platform to Android. In Player Settings, set a unique package name because the device uses it to identify and install your app. Set Minimum A P I Level to Android 7.0 or higher, since ARCore requires newer APIs. Under Other Settings, set Scripting Backend to IL2CPP and enable the ARM64 architecture so the binary meets modern platform requirements. Disable Auto Graphics A P I if you need to specify OpenGLES3 and Vulkan explicitly. Texture compression like ASTC is recommended for many devices. A concrete example is building com. yourcompany. myfirstarapp with IL2CPP and ARM64; if you leave Mono and only x86 enabled, the APK may fail on many devices. A common misconception is that default player settings suffice — for XR you must explicitly choose scripting backend and architectures. After changing settings, switch platform completes library reimports; expect longer Editor operations. These settings ensure your app can initialize ARCore and provide a stable runtime on Android devices.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Build & Player Settings
Android build configuration
Switch platform then configure Player Settings under Other Settings for ARCore compatibility.
Key fields
  • Company Name & Product Name — app identity for stores and device installs.
  • Package Name — a unique id such as com.yourcompany.myfirstarapp.
  • Minimum API Level — Android 7.0 (API 24) or above for ARCore support.
  • Scripting Backend — IL2CPP; Architecture — ARM64.
  • Graphics/API — consider OpenGLES3 and Vulkan; disable Auto Graphics API to control selection.
Performance tip
For mobile AR, use ASTC texture compression when appropriate and strip unused engine features to keep APK size and memory modest.
Comparison: Common mistakes
Default Player Settings
- May use Mono and not include ARM64, causing install failures on modern devices.
Correct XR Settings
- IL2CPP and ARM64 enabled, package name unique, minimum API set to 24+, initialize XR on startup.
Concrete example
Set com.cohortia.myfirstar as the Package Name, Minimum API Level to API 24, Scripting Backend to IL2CPP and check ARM64. Then build an APK and test plane detection on a device with ARCore support.
Key Takeaway

Explicitly set scripting backend and architectures for Android builds targeting AR; defaults may not meet device requirements.

screens.title: AR Scene Essentials: AR Session & AR Session Origin
screens.narratorSegment: AR Session and AR Session Origin are the foundational GameObjects for any AR Foundation scene. The AR Session manages the lifecycle of AR features such as starting and stopping tracking. It controls the connection to the device's AR runtime. The AR Session Origin, on the other hand, maps tracking data into Unity world space and typically contains the AR Camera. This separation is important: the session is the runtime manager, while the origin is the spatial transform that moves content to match the physical world. A concrete setup: in an empty scene delete the default camera and light, then add XR > AR Session and XR > AR Session Origin. Add AR Plane Manager and AR Raycast Manager to the AR Session Origin so the scene can detect planes and raycast against them. A common misconception is to place plane manager on the AR Session instead of the origin; placing managers on the origin ensures plane transforms align with the camera and other content. Finally, attach an AR-capable camera within AR Session Origin. This arrangement lets you instantiate prefabs in world space that remain correctly positioned as tracking updates arrive.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › AR Session & Origin
AR Session vs AR Session Origin
Understand lifecycle and world mapping so placed objects remain aligned with the physical environment.
AR Session
Manages starting and stopping tracking and connects to the device AR runtime. Think of it as the session controller that enables AR features.
AR Session Origin
Transforms AR coordinate space into Unity world space and usually contains the AR Camera, AR Plane Manager, and AR Raycast Manager.
Concrete example
Add AR Session and AR Session Origin, then add AR Plane Manager and AR Raycast Manager to the origin. Instantiate a prefab at hit poses returned by raycast to place a cube on a detected plane.
Visual: relationship
AR Session
lifecycle
AR Session Origin
camera & managers
Common mistake
Putting plane and raycast managers on a separate root not aligned with the origin can lead to mismatched coordinates and objects appearing offset from detected surfaces.
Key Takeaway

Use AR Session to manage runtime and AR Session Origin to host camera and spatial managers so world mapping is consistent.

screens.title: PlaceOnPlane.cs — Instantiating a Prefab with Touch
screens.narratorSegment: This script demonstrates a simple interaction: when the user taps the screen, perform a raycast into the AR scene and instantiate a prefab at the closest hit pose. The core components are the ARRaycastManager and a reference to the prefab. In Awake we cache the raycast manager with GetComponent, ensuring our script is attached to the AR Session Origin so it can access the manager. In Update we check for a touch and only proceed on the began phase to avoid repeated placements. The Raycast call requests hits of type PlaneWithinPolygon and returns sorted hits; we use the first hit's pose to position the instantiated object. A concrete example is placing a cube prefab when a plane is tapped. A common misconception is to perform the raycast against the camera instead of using ARRaycastManager, which may bypass AR Foundation's correct coordinate mapping. Attach this script to AR Session Origin and assign your prefab in the Inspector. When deployed to a device with ARCore enabled, tapping a detected plane will place the cube. Consider adding simple UX like limiting placement count or providing undo to avoid accidental clutter.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › PlaceOnPlane Script
PlaceOnPlane.cs
Instantiate a prefab at a detected plane position when the user taps the screen.
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARFoundation;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARSubsystems;

public class PlaceOnPlane : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField]
    GameObject m_PlacedPrefab; // Assign your Cube Prefab here in the Inspector

    private ARRaycastManager m_RaycastManager;
    private static List<ARRaycastHit> s_Hits = new List<ARRaycastHit>();

    void Awake()
    {
        m_RaycastManager = GetComponent<ARRaycastManager>();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.touchCount > 0)
        {
            Touch touch = Input.GetTouch(0);
            if (touch.phase == TouchPhase.Began)
            {
                if (m_RaycastManager.Raycast(touch.position, s_Hits, TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon))
                {
                    var hitPose = s_Hits[0].pose;
                    Instantiate(m_PlacedPrefab, hitPose.position, hitPose.rotation);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
Explanation
  • ARRaycastManager handles AR raycasts into detected trackables like planes.
  • TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon ensures hits are inside detected plane boundaries.
  • Instantiate uses the hit pose position and rotation so objects orient with the surface.
Concrete scenario
Build and run on an ARCore-compatible Android device; tap a detected plane and check that the cube prefab appears and stays anchored to the surface as you move the phone.
Common mistake
Forgetting to assign the prefab in the Inspector. The script will run but nothing appears. Also ensure ARRaycastManager component exists on the same GameObject.
Key Takeaway

Use ARRaycastManager and trackable hits to reliably place prefabs; attach components and assign references before testing on device.

screens.title: ARPlaneDebugger.cs — Visualizing Plane Events
screens.narratorSegment: ARPlaneDebugger shows how to subscribe to ARPlaneManager events to visualize when planes are added, updated, or removed. The script requires an ARPlaneManager component and a plane visualization prefab. In Awake we obtain the ARPlaneManager with GetComponent and add a handler to the planesChanged event so we respond to the runtime's discovery of trackables. For each added plane, instantiate a visual prefab and parent it to the plane's transform so the visual follows plane updates. For removed planes, destroy the visual child if it exists. A concrete example: the ARPlaneVisualizerPrefab could be a simple mesh that highlights the detected plane so you can see where raycasts will hit. A common misconception is to create visual objects that are not parented to the ARPlane; without parenting the visuals won't move or disappear with the tracked plane. Remember to remove the event handler in OnDestroy to avoid memory leaks when scenes change. This pattern keeps visualization tied to the lifecycle of AR planes and makes debugging detection robust for testing on device. In practical terms, listen to plane events and create visual plane prefabs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › ARPlaneDebugger Script
ARPlaneDebugger.cs
Visualize added, updated, and removed planes by instantiating and parenting a prefab to each ARPlane.
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARFoundation;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARSubsystems;

[RequireComponent(typeof(ARPlaneManager))]
public class ARPlaneDebugger : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField]
    GameObject m_PlanePrefab; // Assign a simple plane visualization prefab here

    ARPlaneManager m_ARPlaneManager;

    void Awake()
    {
        m_ARPlaneManager = GetComponent<ARPlaneManager>();
        m_ARPlaneManager.planesChanged += OnPlanesChanged;
    }

    void OnDestroy()
    {
        m_ARPlaneManager.planesChanged -= OnPlanesChanged;
    }

    void OnPlanesChanged(ARPlanesChangedEventArgs args)
    {
        foreach (var plane in args.added)
        {
            Debug.Log($"New plane detected: {plane.trackableId}");
            if (m_PlanePrefab != null)
            {
                GameObject planeVisual = Instantiate(m_PlanePrefab, plane.transform.position, plane.transform.rotation);
                planeVisual.transform.SetParent(plane.transform);
            }
        }
        foreach (var plane in args.updated)
        {
            Debug.Log($"Plane updated: {plane.trackableId}");
        }
        foreach (var plane in args.removed)
        {
            Debug.Log($"Plane removed: {plane.trackableId}");
            if (plane.transform.childCount > 0)
            {
                Destroy(plane.transform.GetChild(0).gameObject);
            }
        }
    }
}
Explanation
  • Subscribe to planesChanged to react to runtime plane additions, updates, and removals.
  • Parent visuals to the ARPlane transform so they move and update with the tracking system.
  • Unsubscribe in OnDestroy to prevent lingering event references when scenes unload.
Concrete setup
Create a Plane visual prefab with ARPlaneMeshVisualizer and optional material. Assign it to m_PlanePrefab and test by moving the device until planes appear in the Editor logs or on the connected device screen.
Common mistake
Not parenting the visual to the plane. Visuals not parented to the ARPlane won't follow updates and can remain in the scene after the plane is removed.
Key Takeaway

Use ARPlaneManager events and parent visualization prefabs to keep debug visuals in sync with tracked planes during testing.

Activity: Build and run a simple AR app
Follow these steps to confirm your project is AR-ready and the runtime initializes on an Android device.
Steps
  1. Create new 3D Core project and open Package Manager → Unity Registry.
  2. Install XR Plugin Management, AR Foundation, and ARCore XR Plugin.
  3. Enable ARCore under Edit → Project Settings → XR Plugin Management → Android.
  4. File → Build Settings → Switch Platform to Android.
  5. Player Settings: set Package Name, Minimum API Level to API 24+, IL2CPP, enable ARM64.
  6. Add XR → AR Session and XR → AR Session Origin. Add plane and raycast managers to the origin.
  7. Create cube prefab, attach PlaceOnPlane script and assign prefab.
  8. Build And Run to an ARCore-compatible Android device and test plane tap placement.
What success looks like
A cube appears at the tap location on a detected plane and remains anchored as you move the device.
Checklist
  • ARCore enabled in XR Plugin Management.
  • Package Name unique and Minimum API set.
  • IL2CPP and ARM64 enabled.
  • ARRaycastManager present and prefab assigned.
Troubleshoot
If build fails, confirm Android Build Support module is installed in the Editor. If app runs but plane detection fails, confirm provider installation and device AR support.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When an XR app fails to initialize or a build fails, there are predictable configuration causes to check first. Start by confirming you switched the active platform in Build Settings; many plugin provider toggles appear only for the active platform. Next, open XR Plugin Management and ensure the correct provider is enabled for that platform — installation alone doesn’t enable it. Verify Player Settings: a wrong scripting backend or missing ARM64 option causes APKs to reject installation on modern devices. Also confirm Minimum A P I Level meets provider requirements. Check that you installed Editor modules like Android Build Support for building APKs. For runtime problems, open the Editor log or Android logcat to see missing native bindings or exceptions — these often point to disabled providers or missing initialization. A concrete troubleshooting example: a blank Quest app often indicates the Android tab lacks an active Oculus or OpenXR provider or that Initialize XR on Startup is unchecked. For safety: remind users to clear physical space for AR and VR testing, and use comfortable movement to reduce motion sickness in VR. These checks quickly isolate common errors so you can iterate.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn how to configure a Unity project for both AR and VR, install the essential packages, set up XR Plugin Management, and prepare build and player settings so your app can run on Android devices and PC or Quest headsets. We'll also walk through creating a minimal AR scene that places objects on detected planes and a simple VR rig using the XR Interaction Toolkit. This setup work is crucial: without the right packages and provider selections, Unity cannot communicate with ARCore, ARKit, OpenXR, or device-specific runtimes. For example, AR Foundation provides the common A P I but needs platform providers like ARCore or ARKit to actually detect planes on a phone. Throughout this lesson you'll see concrete steps to avoid common mistakes such as forgetting to switch platforms, not enabling the correct plugin provider, or misconfiguring scripting and architecture for Android builds. By the end you'll understand the project-level decisions that let your scenes initialize XR at startup and run reliably on target hardware. Think about a simple test: placing a cube on a detected plane. If that works on your device, your pipeline is correctly configured.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to prepare Unity projects for AR and VR. That means you will install and manage the right packages through the Package Manager, configure XR Plugin Management for each target platform, and set Android build and player settings so ARCore works correctly. You'll also create an AR scene that detects planes and lets you instantiate prefabs with a tap, and build a minimal VR scene using XR Interaction Toolkit and XR Origin. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: package installation, provider selection, platform-specific settings, and scene-level components. For example, installing AR Foundation alone is not enough to run AR on Android — you will learn to install ARCore XR Plugin and enable it in Project Settings so runtime services can start. You'll also practice a small build-and-deploy activity: configure the package name, set IL2CPP and ARM64, and build an APK to test on an Android device. These skills reduce the common errors developers face and get you from an empty project to a running AR or VR prototype.

This second objectives slide expands the chapter into practical skills you can verify. You will learn to prepare player settings such as package name, minimum A P I level, and graphics APIs which are essential for ARCore on Android. You will configure scripting backend to IL2CPP and enable ARM64, because many devices require 64‑bit binaries. You'll also add a minimal VR rig using XR Interaction Toolkit and an XR Origin so you can test a desktop or Quest experience. Finally, you'll practice basic troubleshooting: recognizing when the app fails because the wrong provider is enabled or because the active platform hasn't been switched. Each skill includes a short verification step so you can confirm success. For example, validating that "Initialize XR on Startup" is checked and that the Android tab lists ARCore will confirm the runtime will initialize when the app launches. These hands-on checks reduce build failures and speed iteration.

The Package Manager is where Unity grows into an XR-capable editor. Think of it as a repository of editor extensions and runtime libraries that add AR and VR features. Start by switching the Package Manager view to the Unity Registry so you see official packages. The key packages to install are XR Plugin Management, which centralizes provider configuration; AR Foundation, which offers a cross-platform AR A P I; OpenXR, which gives a device-agnostic VR interface; and the platform-specific provider packages like ARCore XR Plugin for Android and ARKit XR Plugin for iOS. Install the XR Interaction Toolkit if you'll build VR interactions. A concrete example: installing AR Foundation alone won’t make plane detection work on Android — ARCore XR Plugin is needed so the phone’s AR runtime can be accessed. A common misconception is that a single package covers all platforms; instead, AR Foundation is the bridge and platform providers are the engines. After installation, verify package versions and restart the editor if package dependencies require it. This reduces mysterious runtime errors and ensures the Package Manager shows the provider packages as available in Project Settings when you configure XR Plugin Management.

XR Plugin Management is the bridge between Unity and device runtimes. Open Edit > Project Settings > XR Plugin Management and you'll see tabs for each target platform, such as Android and Standalone. For an Android AR build, select the Android tab and enable ARCore. For Quest or other Meta devices running Android, enable Oculus or OpenXR depending on your chosen provider. On Standalone, enable OpenXR or Oculus for PC-focused VR. A concrete example: if you want to target Meta Quest using OpenXR, enable OpenXR in the Android tab and also configure any necessary runtime features in the OpenXR settings. A frequent misconception is to only install the plugin but forget to toggle it on per-platform; remember that installation makes providers available, while XR Plugin Management activates them for a specific platform. Also check the option to initialize XR on startup for the platform — without it, you may need to initialize subsystems manually in code. Finally, after changing providers, restart the Editor when prompted to ensure native bindings are loaded. This step often resolves mysterious initialization failures during builds.

Build Settings and Player Settings determine whether an Android APK will install and run AR features. To prepare for ARCore, open File > Build Settings and switch the platform to Android. In Player Settings, set a unique package name because the device uses it to identify and install your app. Set Minimum A P I Level to Android 7.0 or higher, since ARCore requires newer APIs. Under Other Settings, set Scripting Backend to IL2CPP and enable the ARM64 architecture so the binary meets modern platform requirements. Disable Auto Graphics A P I if you need to specify OpenGLES3 and Vulkan explicitly. Texture compression like ASTC is recommended for many devices. A concrete example is building com. yourcompany. myfirstarapp with IL2CPP and ARM64; if you leave Mono and only x86 enabled, the APK may fail on many devices. A common misconception is that default player settings suffice — for XR you must explicitly choose scripting backend and architectures. After changing settings, switch platform completes library reimports; expect longer Editor operations. These settings ensure your app can initialize ARCore and provide a stable runtime on Android devices.

AR Session and AR Session Origin are the foundational GameObjects for any AR Foundation scene. The AR Session manages the lifecycle of AR features such as starting and stopping tracking. It controls the connection to the device's AR runtime. The AR Session Origin, on the other hand, maps tracking data into Unity world space and typically contains the AR Camera. This separation is important: the session is the runtime manager, while the origin is the spatial transform that moves content to match the physical world. A concrete setup: in an empty scene delete the default camera and light, then add XR > AR Session and XR > AR Session Origin. Add AR Plane Manager and AR Raycast Manager to the AR Session Origin so the scene can detect planes and raycast against them. A common misconception is to place plane manager on the AR Session instead of the origin; placing managers on the origin ensures plane transforms align with the camera and other content. Finally, attach an AR-capable camera within AR Session Origin. This arrangement lets you instantiate prefabs in world space that remain correctly positioned as tracking updates arrive.

This script demonstrates a simple interaction: when the user taps the screen, perform a raycast into the AR scene and instantiate a prefab at the closest hit pose. The core components are the ARRaycastManager and a reference to the prefab. In Awake we cache the raycast manager with GetComponent, ensuring our script is attached to the AR Session Origin so it can access the manager. In Update we check for a touch and only proceed on the began phase to avoid repeated placements. The Raycast call requests hits of type PlaneWithinPolygon and returns sorted hits; we use the first hit's pose to position the instantiated object. A concrete example is placing a cube prefab when a plane is tapped. A common misconception is to perform the raycast against the camera instead of using ARRaycastManager, which may bypass AR Foundation's correct coordinate mapping. Attach this script to AR Session Origin and assign your prefab in the Inspector. When deployed to a device with ARCore enabled, tapping a detected plane will place the cube. A common misconception is to create visual objects that are not parented to the ARPlane; without parenting the visuals won't move or disappear with the tracked plane. Remember to remove the event handler in OnDestroy to avoid memory leaks when scenes change.
